steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on path-based trajectory prediction (PBP) for autonomous driving. Explain why trajectory prediction is hard and why map compliance matters, how prior methods use HD maps, what our path-based decoder does differently, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Trajectory prediction for autonomous driving and why it is hard
- HD maps and map compliance
- Prior work 1: HD map as model input
- Prior work 2: goal-based prediction
- Our approach: path-based prediction
- Implementation, results and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Trajectory prediction for autonomous driving and why it is hard
  - AVs need to predict surrounding agents' trajectories: safe navigation, smooth ride
  - inherent uncertainty of the future
  - trajectories highly non-linear over long horizons
  - multimodal: multiple plausible goals, various paths to each
- HD maps and map compliance
  - motion not unconstrained: vehicles follow lane direction, legal turns/lane changes, stop at stop signs/crosswalks
  - bicyclists in bike lane; pedestrians on sidewalks and crosswalks
  - HD maps represent these constraints; critical component of AV datasets
  - prior works: key requirement = map-compliant trajectories (no going off-road, no traffic rule violations, long horizons)
  - example: non-compliant prediction into oncoming lane -> ego vehicle brakes hard / dangerous maneuvers
  - map compliance w.r.t. HD map central to our approach and evaluation
- Prior work 1: HD map as model input
  - early: rasterized HD maps + CNN encoders
  - recent: vectorized maps via PointNet encoders, graph neural networks, transformer layers
  - map encoding -> multimodal prediction header -> K trajectories + probabilities
  - drawback: complex one-to-many mapping from scene context to futures -> non-map-compliant predictions
- Prior work 2: goal-based prediction
  - each mode tied to 2D goal location sampled from HD map
  - discrete distribution over goals, then trajectories conditioned on each goal
  - simpler mapping for header; more interpretable modes
  - but 2D goals = weak inductive bias -> imprecise trajectories per goal
- Our approach: path-based prediction
  - improve on goal-based prediction; condition on reference paths, not 2D goals
  - reference path = segment of lane centerline near agent of interest that it may follow over the horizon
  - path classifier: discrete distribution over candidate paths; trajectory completion module in Frenet frame; Figure 1
  - advantage 1: path features instead of goal features -> more informative, more map-compliant over long horizons
  - advantage 2: Frenet frame -> much lower variance than Cartesian (varying lane locations, curvatures), generalizes to novel layouts
- Implementation, results and contributions
  - decoder modular; works with any scene encoder: VectorNet, LaneGCN, Scene Transformer, Wayformer
  - built on HiVT encoder: competitive on Argoverse, public code
  - Argoverse: competitive minADE, minFDE, miss rate; much better map compliance than HiVT baseline and goal-based
  - contribution: novel PBP approach improving on goal-based prediction
  - contribution: PBP decoder on HiVT -> best map compliance on Argoverse leaderboard, competitive error metrics
  - contribution: extensive ablations of decoders on Argoverse validation set

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous vehicles need to be able to predict the trajectories of the agents around them, so that they can navigate safely through traffic and also give passengers a smooth ride. This is a challenging task because predicting the future is inherently uncertain. Agent trajectories are often highly non-linear over long prediction horizons. Also the distribution of future trajectories is multimodal, since in a given scene an agent could have multiple plausible goals and it could take various paths to each goal.

Even with these challenges, the motion of agents is not completely unconstrained. Vehicles usually follow the direction of motion of their lanes, they make legal turns and lane changes, and they stop at stop signs and crosswalks. Bicyclists usually use the bike lane and pedestrians usually walk on sidewalks and crosswalks. High-definition (HD) maps of traffic scenes represent these constraints on agent motion efficiently, and so they have been a critical component of autonomous driving datasets. Many prior works have shown that a key requirement of trajectory prediction for a real-world autonomous driving system is to predict map-compliant trajectories, which are trajectories that don't go off-road or violate traffic rules over long prediction horizons. For example, if a non-map-compliant trajectory that encroaches into the oncoming traffic lane is predicted incorrectly, it could make the ego vehicle brake hard or even make dangerous maneuvers on the road. So map compliance of the predictions w.r.t. the provided HD map is central to our approach and to our experimental evaluation.

There are two different ways prior works have used HD maps for trajectory prediction. The first is that the HD map is often used as an input to the model. Early works use rasterized HD maps with CNN encoders. More recent works encode vectorized HD maps directly, using PointNet encoders, graph neural networks or transformer layers. Then a multimodal prediction header uses the map encoding to output K trajectories and their probabilities. The drawback of multimodal prediction headers is that they have to learn a complex one-to-many mapping from the whole scene context to multiple future trajectories, and this often leads to non-map-compliant predictions.

- Prior work 2: goal-based prediction
  - each mode tied to 2D goal location sampled from HD map
  - discrete distribution over goals, then trajectories conditioned on each goal
  - simpler mapping for header; more interpretable modes
  - but 2D goals = weak inductive bias -> imprecise trajectories per goal

  - improve on goal-based prediction; condition on reference paths, not 2D goals
  - reference path = segment of lane centerline near agent of interest that it may follow over the horizon
  - path classifier: discrete distribution over candidate paths; trajectory completion module in Frenet frame; Figure 1
  - advantage 1: path features instead of goal features -> more informative, more map-compliant over long horizons
  - advantage 2: Frenet frame -> much lower variance than Cartesian (varying lane locations, curvatures), generalizes to novel layouts

  - built on HiVT encoder: competitive on Argoverse, public code
  - Argoverse: competitive minADE, minFDE, miss rate; much better map compliance than HiVT baseline and goal-based
  - contribution: novel PBP approach improving on goal-based prediction
  - contribution: PBP decoder on HiVT -> best map compliance on Argoverse leaderboard, competitive error metrics

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Autonomous vehicles need to be able to predict the trajectories of the agents around them, so that they can navigate safely through traffic and also give passengers a smooth ride. This is a challenging task because predicting the future is inherently uncertain. Agent trajectories are often highly non-linear over long prediction horizons. Also the distribution of future trajectories is multimodal, since in a given scene an agent could have multiple plausible goals and it could take various paths to each goal.

Even with these challenges, the motion of agents is not completely unconstrained. Vehicles usually follow the direction of motion of their lanes, they make legal turns and lane changes, and they stop at stop signs and crosswalks. Bicyclists usually use the bike lane and pedestrians usually walk on sidewalks and crosswalks. High-definition (HD) maps of traffic scenes represent these constraints on agent motion efficiently, and so they have been a critical component of autonomous driving datasets. Many prior works have shown that a key requirement of trajectory prediction for a real-world autonomous driving system is to predict map-compliant trajectories, which are trajectories that don't go off-road or violate traffic rules over long prediction horizons. For example, if a non-map-compliant trajectory that encroaches into the oncoming traffic lane is predicted incorrectly, it could make the ego vehicle brake hard or even make dangerous maneuvers on the road. So map compliance of the predictions w.r.t. the provided HD map is central to our approach and to our experimental evaluation.

There are two different ways prior works have used HD maps for trajectory prediction. The first is that the HD map is often used as an input to the model. Early works use rasterized HD maps with CNN encoders. More recent works encode vectorized HD maps directly, using PointNet encoders, graph neural networks or transformer layers. Then a multimodal prediction header uses the map encoding to output K trajectories and their probabilities. The drawback of multimodal prediction headers is that they have to learn a complex one-to-many mapping from the whole scene context to multiple future trajectories, and this often leads to non-map-compliant predictions.

To address this, a few recent works also use the HD map for goal-based prediction. Goal-based prediction models associate each mode of the trajectory distribution with a 2D goal location that is sampled from the HD map. They predict a discrete distribution over the sampled goals, and then they predict trajectories conditioned on each goal. This makes the mapping the prediction header learns simpler, and it also makes each mode of the distribution more interpretable. But 2D goal locations are a weak inductive bias for conditioning predictions, and they can lead to imprecise trajectories for each goal.

In this work we want to improve on goal-based trajectory prediction. We argue that the right HD map element to condition predicted trajectories on is reference paths and not 2D goals. We define reference paths as segments of lane centerlines that are close to the agent of interest and that the agent may follow over the prediction horizon. We propose a novel path classifier that predicts a discrete probability distribution over the candidate reference paths, and a trajectory completion module that predicts trajectories conditioned on each path in the Frenet frame. An overview of our approach is in Figure 1. Our approach has two key advantages over goal-based prediction:

- Path features instead of goal features: We condition the predicted trajectories on feature descriptors of the whole reference path and not just on 2D goal locations. This feature descriptor is more informative, and it leads to more map-compliant trajectories over longer prediction horizons than goal-based prediction.

- Prediction in the Frenet frame: With the reference paths we can predict trajectories in the Frenet frame relative to the path. The Cartesian frame has varying lane locations and curvatures, and compared to it predictions in the Frenet frame have much lower variance, which leads to more map-compliant trajectories that generalize better to novel scene layouts.

Our path-based trajectory decoder is modular by design, so it could be used with any existing scene encoder, such as VectorNet, LaneGCN, Scene Transformer, Wayformer, etc. Here we build the decoder on top of the HiVT encoder, which was recently proposed and achieved competitive results on the Argoverse dataset, and which has a publicly available code base. On the Argoverse dataset, our results show that the path-based decoder is competitive in terms of the standard minADE, minFDE, and miss rate metrics, and it significantly outperforms the HiVT baseline and goal-based prediction on map compliance metrics.

Our contributions are:

- We propose a novel path-based trajectory prediction (PBP) approach that improves on traditional goal-based prediction.

- We applied our PBP trajectory decoder on top of the HiVT scene encoder. The model we get achieves the best map compliance metric on the Argoverse leaderboard and is competitive on prediction error metrics.

- We present extensive ablation studies that compare different trajectory decoder approaches on the Argoverse validation set.

steps.text:
To safely navigate through traffic while offering passengers a smooth ride, autonomous vehicles need to be able to predict the trajectories of surrounding agents. Predicting the future is inherently uncertain, which makes this a challenging task. Agent trajectories tend to be highly non-linear over long prediction horizons. Additionally, the distribution of future trajectories is multimodal; in a given scene an agent could have multiple plausible goals and could take various paths to each of them.

In spite of these challenges, agent motion is not completely unconstrained. Vehicles tend to follow the direction of motion of their lanes, make legal turns and lane changes, and stop at stop signs and crosswalks. Bicyclists tend to use the bike lane, and pedestrians tend to walk along sidewalks and crosswalks. High-definition (HD) maps of traffic scenes efficiently represent such constraints on agent motion and have therefore been a critical component of autonomous driving datasets [1,2,3,4,5]. In fact, many prior works [6,7,8,9,10,11,12] have shown that a key requirement of trajectory prediction for a real-world autonomous driving system is to predict map-compliant trajectories – trajectories that don’t go off-road or violate traffic rules over long prediction horizons. For example, incorrectly predicting a non-map-compliant trajectory that encroaches into the oncoming traffic lane could cause the ego vehicle to brake hard or even make dangerous maneuvers on the road. As a result, prediction map compliance w.r.t. the provided HD map is central to our proposed approach and experimental evaluation.

Prior works have leveraged HD maps for trajectory prediction in two distinct ways. First, the HD map is often used as an input to the model. Early works [13,14,15] use rasterized HD maps and CNN encoders. However, 2D goal locations are a weak inductive bias for conditioning predictions, and may lead to imprecise trajectories for each goal.

We argue that reference paths rather than 2D goals are the appropriate HD map element on which to condition predicted trajectories. We propose a novel path classifier that predicts a discrete probability distribution over the candidate reference paths, and a trajectory completion module that predicts trajectories conditioned on each path in the Frenet frame. - 2. Prediction in the Frenet frame: The reference paths allow us to predict trajectories in the Frenet frame relative to the path. Compared to the Cartesian frame with its varying lane locations and curvatures, predictions in the Frenet frame have much lower variance, leading to more map-compliant trajectories that generalize better to novel scene layouts.

Our path-based trajectory decoder is modular by design and could be used with any existing scene encoder such as VectorNet [17], LaneGCN [18], Scene Transformer [19], Wayformer [21], etc. Here, we build our decoder on top of the recently proposed HiVT encoder [22], which achieved competitive results on the Argoverse dataset [1] and has a publicly available code base. Our results on the Argoverse dataset show that the path-based decoder achieves competitive performance on the standard minADE, minFDE, and miss rate metrics, while significantly outperforming the HiVT baseline and goal-based prediction on map compliance metrics.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We propose a novel path-based trajectory prediction (PBP) approach that improves upon traditional goal-based prediction.

- • We applied our PBP trajectory decoder on top of the HiVT [22] scene encoder. The resulting model achieves the best map compliance metric on the Argoverse leaderboard while remaining competitive on prediction error metrics.

- • We present extensive ablation studies comparing different trajectory decoder approaches on the Argoverse validation set.
